subject: english
title: D：思考能力

content.summary: 本課把英文閱讀變成可檢查的推理：學習者從校園二手書交換公告、學生訊息與午餐方案表中，分辨直接事實、線索支持的推論與文本沒有提供的未知資訊，再用英文說明證據、條件與結論界線。

sections.heading: 學習目標
sections.body: 能使用 who、what、when、where、why、how 釐清問題，從英文資料找出直接證據，並以完整句子說明推論與限制。

sections.heading: 學習流程
sections.body: 先辨認任務與關鍵限制，再把資訊分成 Fact、Inference、Unknown；接著用 because、so、but 或 if 連起證據與結論，最後檢查語氣是否把可能性誇大成確定性。

sections.heading: 常見錯誤
sections.body: 不要把單一數字擴大成 everyone 的規則，也不要替文本補上沒有說出的理由；may、might、only、first 與 if 都可能改變答案的範圍或確定程度。

sections.heading: 自我檢核
sections.body: 在新公告或比較表中，能指出支持結論的字詞、數字或條件，並用英文寫出資料能證明什麼、不能證明什麼。

studyHighlights: 先圈出與「思考能力」直接相關的條件。
用自己的話說出判斷依據，不靠答案位置或關鍵字猜測。
回到原題檢查結論是否符合所有限制與資料。

body.heading: A poster is not the whole story
body.body: Imagine a poster near the school gate: “Book Swap Day—Friday, 12:30–1:30, Room 204. Bring one clean book and take one book.” A classmate says, “Everyone can take as many books as they want.” Read the poster again. The words one clean book and take one book are direct evidence; the classmate’s claim is not. This is the first habit of thinking in English: do not choose an answer merely because it sounds reasonable. Ask who is involved, what action is required, when and where it happens, and which words support your answer. If the poster does not tell us whether magazines are welcome, write “The poster does not tell us” rather than inventing a rule. That sentence is accurate reading, not a failure.

body.heading: Turn information into a thinking map
body.body: While reading, make three columns: Facts, Inferences, and Unknowns. Facts are words directly stated, such as “The exchange is in Room 204.” An inference is a conclusion supported by clues, such as “Students should prepare a book before Friday.” An unknown is information the text never supplies, such as whether comic books are accepted. Keep grammar visible when you explain the link. Use because for a reason—“Mia brings a book because the notice asks each visitor to bring one.” Use so for a result—“The room is open at lunchtime, so students can visit after class.” Use but to hold two truths together—“The notice gives a time, but it gives no rule for late visitors.” A thoughtful reader shows how a sentence is connected to evidence instead of merely collecting vocabulary.

body.heading: Test a conclusion against a message
body.body: Read this original student-council message: “We have received 36 books for Friday’s swap. The first 20 visitors may choose a second book after they exchange one. Please put science, stories, and art books on the labeled tables. If rain continues, the event will move to the library.” “Every visitor may take two books” is false because first 20 sets a limit. “The event might not be in Room 204” is a reasonable possibility when an earlier notice named Room 204, because if rain continues can change the place. “There are 36 science books” is unknown: 36 is the total, not a category count. The words may, first 20, and if control the strength and range of each conclusion. Explain your choice by naming the clue and its job.

body.heading: Do not fill in a missing reason
body.body: Study this message: “Kai cannot join the swap at noon because he has a music lesson. He asks Lena to leave a history book for him. Lena replies, ‘I can save one if it is still there at 1:00.’” Underline cannot, because, if, and still. Kai’s music lesson and his request are facts. The book’s availability at 1:00 is uncertain. Compare “Lena saves the book” with “Lena may save the book if it is still there.” The second sentence preserves the condition. If a question asks why Lena is late but the message gives no reason, write “The announcement does not explain why Lena might be late.” Do not copy a familiar sentence and add a reason simply because it sounds complete. Accurate English sometimes states a boundary instead of pretending to know more.

body.heading: Compare choices without declaring one best for all
body.body: The eco club offers two lunch plans. Plan A costs 40 dollars, uses a reusable box, and must be ordered one day early. Plan B costs 30 dollars, uses a paper box, and can be ordered the same day. “Plan B is better for everyone” is too broad. A lower price may matter to one student, while less waste may matter to another. Write: “Plan A is more expensive than Plan B because it costs 40 dollars, but it creates less packaging waste.” Then state the missing information: “We do not know whether the reusable box can be washed at school.” Before accepting best or everyone, ask best for whom, under which condition, and according to which evidence. This is how a reading strategy transfers from an announcement to a comparison table.

body.heading: Make your reasoning visible
body.body: Revise one answer with the Evidence–Link–Limit check. Evidence asks which word, number, time, or condition supports the claim. Link asks which connector explains the relationship: because, so, but, or if. Limit asks what the source cannot prove. A careful answer is: “The first 20 visitors may choose a second book because the announcement gives that limit. It does not say that later visitors can do so.” Remember that may and might show possibility, must shows a requirement, only sets a boundary, and if opens a condition. Thinking ability is not an extra trick after grammar; it is the habit of choosing words whose certainty and scope match the evidence.

summary: 用 who、what、when、where、why、how 釐清題目真正要求的資訊。
將英文資料分成直接事實、線索支持的推論，以及文本沒有提供的未知資訊。
辨認 only、first、may、must、if 等限制與條件字，避免把可能性說成確定事實。
用 because、so、but 說明證據關係，並檢查結論是否超出資料範圍。

exitCheck.prompt: Why is “Every visitor may take two books” an unsafe conclusion?
exitCheck.expectedEvidence: 能指出 first 20 visitors 的限制，並用英文說明第二本書規則不適用所有訪客。

exitCheck.prompt: Write one sentence that separates a fact from an inference in the lunch-plan comparison.
exitCheck.expectedEvidence: 能指出明示價格或包裝資料，再用 because、but 或 so 說明證據與推論關係。

exitCheck.prompt: What should you write when a source does not provide the reason for an action?
exitCheck.expectedEvidence: 能使用 The text does not explain... 或同等準確句型，避免自行補入未提供的理由。
